repairs.value: Strongest feature: Sechler concedes Pat Tillman’s atheistic self-sacrifice, then distinguishes Christian sacrifice through loving and serving God as the ultimate good, genuinely and directly answering Clifton’s central ethical-life challenge with unusual charity. Principal limitation: The distinction earns 45 for evidential warrant because identifying God as the ultimate good assumes the Christian framework under dispute; Tillman demonstrates atheist sacrifice without showing that divine service adds defensible moral value. Live burden: Sechler needs to explain why serving God improves sacrifice rather than redescribing it within theism, and why that improvement outweighs Clifton’s concern about belief-related costs. Locked score: The 67 reflects a clear, relevant concession-and-reply whose decisive value claim remains unsupported outside the worldview it presupposes.

Strongest feature: Clifton exposes a central motivational tension in Sechler’s account: when self-sacrifice brings guaranteed eternal compensation, surrender may function as long-run self-interest, challenging the superior value of Christian sacrifice. Principal limitation: The conclusion earns 55 for evidential warrant because promised reward does not erase loss, mixed motives, or loving action independent of compensation; Clifton offers no reason every reward-aware sacrifice becomes merely selfish. Live burden: Clifton needs to distinguish reward as a foreseen consequence from reward as the controlling motive, then show why infinite compensation necessarily cancels rather than complicates genuine sacrifice. Locked score: The 72 fits a precise, highly responsive challenge whose conceptual insight is weakened by treating one possible motivational structure as universal.
